pos: n. (an inhabitant of Gilead, east of Jordan)
etymology: From Gilead, the highland region east of the Jordan allotted to Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh. The gentilic marks a man as coming from the rough country across the river — and in Judges it marks two men who judged Israel.
biblical_def: The term identifies men of the trans-Jordan highlands. One is dispatched in a sentence: “And after him arose Jair, a Gileadite, and judged Israel twenty and two years” (Judges 10:3). The other gets three chapters: “Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty man of valour, and he was the son of an harlot: and Gilead begat Jephthah” (Judges 11:1). His origin is given in the same breath as his valour, because his brothers had used it to drive him out and Israel later came begging for him. The Spirit came upon him, Ammon was subdued, and the chapter ends in the worst way a victory can: “That the daughters of Israel went yearly to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in a year” (Judges 11:40). The same region later gives Israel its fiercest prophet, whose home is named in his first appearance: “And Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the inhabitants of Gilead, said unto Ahab, As the LORD God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word” (1 Kings 17:1). Gilead was frontier country, half outside the land proper, and God repeatedly drew from it men the settled tribes would not have chosen.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Gilead as a mountainous region beyond Jordan, famous for its balm, and a Gileadite as one of its inhabitants.
webster_full: GILEAD, n. A mountainous tract beyond Jordan, allotted to Reuben, Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh; noted for its balm.
GENTILE NAME, a name derived from a nation, tribe or country, denoting the place of one's birth or residence.
JUDGE, n. Among the Hebrews, a chief magistrate raised up of God to deliver and rule Israel before the kings.
BALM, n. The sap or juice of trees remarkably odoriferous; the balm of Gilead, famous as a medicine.
FRONTIER, n. The marches; the border, confine or extreme part of a country, bordering on another country.
scriptures: Judges 10:3
And after him arose Jair, a Gileadite, and judged Israel twenty and two years.
Judges 11:1
Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty man of valour, and he was the son of an harlot : and Gilead begat Jephthah. Jephthah:
Judges 11:40
That the daughters of Israel went yearly to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in a year.
1 Kings 17:1

And Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the inhabitants of Gilead, said unto Ahab, As the LORD God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.
corruption_summary: Jephthah is defended as a misunderstood hero or dismissed as a barbarian, and in both cases the plain record of a rash vow and its cost is edited rather than read.
corruption_paragraphs: Two evasions attend Jephthah the Gileadite. The first, well meant, argues that his daughter was devoted to perpetual virginity rather than offered up, softening the text to protect his place in the roll of faith in Hebrews 11. The second dismisses him as a brutal chieftain whose story proves the crudity of the period. Judges does neither. It records that the Spirit of the LORD came upon him, that he delivered Israel, that he made a vow he was under no obligation to make, and that he did with her according to his vow. Scripture honours what God did through him and never excuses what he did.

That combination is the book's method throughout, and it is why Judges is such a corrective to modern hagiography. The men God used are shown with their sins unretouched — Gideon's ephod, Samson's appetites, Jephthah's vow — and the refrain explains the whole era: every man did that which was right in his own eyes. The lesson is not that God endorses His instruments but that He is not limited by them. A Gileadite outcast, the son of a harlot, driven off by his brothers, was raised up to save Israel, and the same book that says so also records what his ignorance of God's law cost his only child.

pos: n. (a woman of Shunem, in Issachar)
etymology: From Shunem, a town in the territory of Issachar near the plain of Jezreel. Two women bear the name in Scripture — Abishag, who attended the dying David, and the unnamed hostess of Elisha.
biblical_def: The word first identifies a young woman brought to a failing king: “So they sought for a fair damsel throughout all the coasts of Israel, and found Abishag a Shunammite, and brought her to the king” (1 Kings 1:3). Her presence marks David's weakness rather than his appetite; the narrative is careful to say the king knew her not. She is in the room for the succession crisis: “And Bathsheba went in unto the king into the chamber: and the king was very old; and Abishag the Shunammite ministered unto the king” (1 Kings 1:15). Adonijah later asks for her, and Solomon reads the request as a claim on the throne and executes him: “And he said, Speak, I pray thee, unto Solomon the king, (for he will not say thee nay,) that he give me Abishag the Shunammite to wife” (1 Kings 2:17). The second Shunammite is the great woman of 2 Kings 4, who built a prophet's chamber, received the promise of a son, lost him, and rode to Carmel to find Elisha. Her answer on the road is one of the great sentences of faith in the Old Testament: “And she answered, It is well” (2 Kings 4:26). She said it with the child lying dead on the prophet's bed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Shunem as a town in the tribe of Issachar, and a Shunammite as a native or inhabitant of Shunem.
webster_full: SHUNEM, n. A city in the tribe of Issachar, in the plain of Esdraelon, near mount Gilboa.
SHUNAMMITE, n. A native or female inhabitant of Shunem.
DAMSEL, n. A young woman; formerly, a young man or woman of noble or genteel extraction.
MINISTER, v.i. To attend and serve; to perform service in any office, sacred or secular.
HOSPITALITY, n. The act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward.
scriptures: 1 Kings 1:3
So they sought for a fair damsel throughout all the coasts of Israel, and found Abishag a Shunammite, and brought her to the king.
1 Kings 1:15
And Bathsheba went in unto the king into the chamber: and the king was very old; and Abishag the Shunammite ministered unto the king.
1 Kings 2:17
And he said, Speak, I pray thee, unto Solomon the king, (for he will not say thee nay,) that he give me Abishag the Shunammite to wife.
2 Kings 4:26
Run now, I pray thee, to meet her, and say unto her, Is it well with thee? is it well with thy husband? is it well with the child? And she answered, It is well.
corruption_summary: The Shunammite of 2 Kings 4 is reduced to a model hostess, and the far harder thing the chapter records — a woman confessing it is well over a dead child — is passed over.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the seriousness of the second Shunammite's faith. She is usually preached as an example of hospitality, which she is: she perceived that Elisha was a holy man of God and built him a chamber with a bed, a table, a stool and a candlestick. But the chapter does not stop at her generosity. It gives her a son by promise, takes him back, and then records her saddling an ass, riding to Carmel, and telling the prophet's servant along the way that it is well — before anything had been put right.

The account is also a rebuke to the notion that faith and grief are alternatives. She says it is well to the servant and then catches Elisha by the feet and says, Did I desire a son of my lord? did I not say, Do not deceive me? She is neither stoic nor faithless; she brings her complaint to the only place it can go and refuses to leave. Scripture gives more space to this woman's persistence than to most kings' reigns, which is its own comment on what it counts worth recording.

pos: n. (a man of Teman, in Edom)
etymology: From Teman, a district of Edom named for a grandson of Esau and proverbial for its wisdom. Eliphaz, the first and most courteous of Job's friends, is identified by it.
biblical_def: The three friends are introduced by their countries: “Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that was come upon him, they came every one from his own place; Eliphaz the Temanite, and Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite: for they had made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him” (Job 2:11). Teman was famous for wisdom — Jeremiah asks whether wisdom is no more in Teman — and Eliphaz speaks first and at greatest length: “Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said” (Job 4:1). His opening is gentle and his theology is the settled doctrine of retribution, which he presses harder each round: “Then answered Eliphaz the Temanite, and said” (Job 15:1). It is to this man that God speaks at the end, and the sentence undoes the whole argument of the book's middle: “And it was so, that after the LORD had spoken these words unto Job, the LORD said to Eliphaz the Temanite, My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath” (Job 42:7). The wisest of the comforters, from the wisest district of Edom, is the man God names first in the rebuke.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Teman as a country and city of Idumea, south of Judea, and a Temanite as an inhabitant of it.
webster_full: TEMAN, n. A city and district of Idumea or Edom, named from a grandson of Esau; proverbial for wisdom.
TEMANITE, n. An inhabitant or native of Teman.
COMFORTER, n. One who administers comfort or consolation; one who strengthens the mind under affliction.
RETRIBUTION, n. Repayment; return accommodated to the action; reward or punishment suited to conduct.
IDUMEA, n. The country of Edom, south and southeast of Judea, settled by the descendants of Esau.
scriptures: Job 2:11

Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that was come upon him, they came every one from his own place; Eliphaz the Temanite, and Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite: for they had made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him.
Job 4:1
Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said,
Job 15:1
Then answered Eliphaz the Temanite, and said,
Job 42:7

And it was so, that after the LORD had spoken these words unto Job, the LORD said to Eliphaz the Temanite, My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath.
corruption_summary: Eliphaz is quoted as though his speeches carried the authority of Scripture's teaching, when Scripture records them accurately and then records God's verdict against them.
corruption_paragraphs: A recurring error in handling Job is to lift a line from Eliphaz — man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward; happy is the man whom God correcteth — and preach it as divine instruction. The verses are inerrantly recorded; the question is whose words they are and what God said about them. The LORD tells Eliphaz plainly that he and his two friends have not spoken of Him the thing that is right. Inspiration guarantees that Scripture reports the speeches exactly. It does not endorse the theology of every speaker it reports, and the book supplies its own key in chapter 42.

What makes the Temanite's error so instructive is how orthodox it looks. God is just; God rewards the righteous and punishes the wicked; therefore a man in ruins should search out his sin. Nearly every clause is true taken alone, and assembled into an accusation against a man God had called perfect and upright they became false witness about God Himself. Reformed theology's insistence that the whole counsel of God be held together, rather than one doctrine pressed into a system that overrides the rest, has few clearer illustrations than Eliphaz of Teman.

pos: n. (a man of the Archi, a clan on the border of Ephraim)
etymology: From Archi, a place on the border of the Josephite territory near Bethel. It identifies one man in Scripture — Hushai, the friend of David, whose counsel saved a fleeing king.
biblical_def: Hushai appears at the lowest point of David's life, as the king climbs the Mount of Olives weeping: “And it came to pass, that when David was come to the top of the mount, where he worshipped God, behold, Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his coat rent, and earth upon his head” (2 Samuel 15:32). David sends him back into the city to defeat the counsel of Ahithophel, and he goes: “And it came to pass, when Hushai the Archite, David's friend, was come unto Absalom, that Hushai said unto Absalom, God save the king, God save the king” (2 Samuel 16:16). The title David's friend is given by the narrator at the moment Hushai appears to change sides. Absalom, having heard Ahithophel advise an immediate pursuit, hesitates: “Then said Absalom, Call now Hushai the Archite also, and let us hear likewise what he saith” (2 Samuel 17:5). Hushai counsels delay, Absalom takes it, and the narrator states who was actually governing the decision: “For the LORD had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that the LORD might bring evil upon Absalom” (2 Samuel 17:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Archi as a place on the borders of Ephraim, and an Archite as an inhabitant of it.
webster_full: ARCHI, n. A place on the confines of the tribe of Ephraim, near Bethel.
ARCHITE, n. A native or inhabitant of Archi.
COUNSEL, n. Advice; opinion or instruction given upon request or otherwise, for directing the judgment or conduct.
FRIEND, n. One who is attached to another by affection; in courts, an officer of confidence attached to the king.
STRATAGEM, n. An artifice, particularly in war; a plan or scheme for deceiving an enemy.
scriptures: 2 Samuel 15:32
And it came to pass, that when David was come to the top of the mount, where he worshipped God, behold, Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his coat rent, and earth upon his head:
2 Samuel 16:16
And it came to pass, when Hushai the Archite, David's friend, was come unto Absalom, that Hushai said unto Absalom, God save the king, God save the king.
2 Samuel 17:5
Then said Absalom, Call now Hushai the Archite also, and let us hear likewise what he saith.
2 Samuel 17:14

And Absalom and all the men of Israel said, The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel. For the LORD had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that the LORD might bring evil upon Absalom.
corruption_summary: The episode is read either as Scripture endorsing deceit or as a difficulty to be explained away, and the narrator's own explanation — that the LORD had appointed to defeat Ahithophel's counsel — is left unused.
corruption_paragraphs: Hushai's mission raises a real question, and it should not be dodged: he entered Absalom's court professing loyalty he did not hold. Some treat this as proof that Scripture approves deception when the cause is good; others strain to show that every word he spoke was technically true. The narrative itself neither commends nor condemns his method. It reports what he did, and then reports the cause of the outcome in words that belong to no human actor: the LORD had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel. The chapter is not offered as an ethics case study. It is offered as an account of providence.

That is the point most worth recovering. Ahithophel's advice was, the text says plainly, good counsel — militarily correct, and it would have killed David that night. It failed not because Hushai out-argued him but because God had appointed that it fail. Ahithophel understood exactly what had happened, went home, set his house in order, and hanged himself. The Reformed doctrine of concurrence is written across this chapter: real men gave real counsel and made free decisions, and the outcome was determined before the first word was spoken.

pos: n. (a man of Tekoa, in Judah)
etymology: From Tekoa, a town in the hill country of Judah about six miles south of Bethlehem. It is the home of Amos the herdman, of the wise woman Joab employed, and of Ira, one of David's mighty men.
biblical_def: The gentilic appears in the military registers. Ira stands in the roll of David's mighty men: “Helez the Paltite, Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite” (2 Samuel 23:26). The Chronicler repeats him in the parallel list: “Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite, Abiezer the Antothite” (1 Chronicles 11:28). And he is given a month in the standing rotation of the kingdom: “The sixth captain for the sixth month was Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite: and in his course were twenty and four thousand” (1 Chronicles 27:9). The same small town produced the herdman whom God took from following the flock: “And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel” (Amos 7:15). Tekoa also supplied the wise woman whom Joab sent to David with a parable to bring Absalom home, and later furnished men who repaired the wall under Nehemiah — though their nobles, the record notes, put not their necks to the work of their Lord. A small place in the Judean hills recurs in Scripture out of all proportion to its size.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Tekoa as a city of Judah, about twelve miles from Jerusalem, the birthplace of the prophet Amos.
webster_full: TEKOA, n. A town in the hill country of Judah, south of Bethlehem; the birthplace of the prophet Amos.
TEKOITE, n. An inhabitant or native of Tekoa.
HERDMAN, n. One employed in tending herds of cattle; a keeper of cattle.
COURSE, n. Order of succession; a series of appointed turns, as of priests or soldiers on duty.
SYCOMORE, n. A tree of the fig kind, whose fruit Amos was a gatherer of.
scriptures: 2 Samuel 23:26
Helez the Paltite, Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite,
1 Chronicles 11:28
Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite, Abiezer the Antothite,
1 Chronicles 27:9
The sixth captain for the sixth month was Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite: and in his course were twenty and four thousand.
Amos 7:15
And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel.
corruption_summary: Lists of names and courses are skipped as filler, and with them goes the doctrine they carry — that God deals with particular men from particular places and keeps their records.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is why Scripture keeps registers at all. A modern reader trained to look for principles finds the courses of 1 Chronicles 27 tedious: twelve captains, twelve months, twenty-four thousand each. What the list asserts is that the kingdom of God is administered in particular men with fathers and hometowns, on particular months, and that God's book records them. The gospel that begins with a genealogy is continuous with this. Names are not the packaging around the message; they are part of the claim that these things happened.

Tekoa is also the standing rebuke to the assumption that God works out of the centres. Amos was a herdman there and a gatherer of sycomore fruit, and he tells Amaziah so flatly: he was no prophet, neither a prophet's son, and the LORD took him from following the flock. Nothing about Tekoa qualified him, and nothing about Jerusalem was required. The men of Tekoa who later repaired two sections of Nehemiah's wall, while their own nobles would not stoop to the work, belong to the same pattern: the record names who laboured and who did not.

pos: n. (the designation of Shemaiah, a false prophet among the exiles)
etymology: Of uncertain place-derivation; some connect it with a Hebrew root meaning to dream, which would make the title a play on the man's trade. It belongs to one man in Scripture, and every mention of it is an indictment.
biblical_def: Jeremiah had written to the exiles in Babylon telling them to build houses and plant gardens, because the captivity would last seventy years. A man among them wrote back to Jerusalem demanding that Jeremiah be silenced, and the LORD answered him by name: “Thus shalt thou also speak to Shemaiah the Nehelamite, saying” (Jeremiah 29:24). The charge is stated exactly: “Send to all them of the captivity, saying, Thus saith the LORD concerning Shemaiah the Nehelamite; Because that Shemaiah hath prophesied unto you, and I sent him not, and he caused you to trust in a lie” (Jeremiah 29:31). The sentence follows: “Therefore thus saith the LORD; Behold, I will punish Shemaiah the Nehelamite, and his seed: he shall not have a man to dwell among this people; neither shall he behold the good that I will do for my people, saith the LORD; because he hath taught rebellion against the LORD” (Jeremiah 29:32). The comfort Shemaiah offered — a short exile, a quick return — was kinder than Jeremiah's seventy years and it was a lie, and God calls the kindness rebellion. In the same letter stands the verse most quoted from Jeremiah: “For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end” (Jeremiah 29:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a false prophet as one who pretends to foretell events or to speak by divine inspiration, without a commission from God.
webster_full: FALSE PROPHET, one who pretends to be commissioned of God, and foretells events which do not come to pass.
PROPHESY, v.i. To utter predictions; to foretell future events; to speak by divine inspiration.
CAPTIVITY, n. The state of being a prisoner, or of being in the power of an enemy; subjection to a foreign power.
REBELLION, n. Open and avowed renunciation of the authority of the government to which one owes allegiance.
PRESUMPTUOUS, a. Bold and confident to excess; arrogant; irreverent with respect to sacred things.
scriptures: Jeremiah 29:24
Thus shalt thou also speak to Shemaiah the Nehelamite, saying,
Jeremiah 29:31

Send to all them of the captivity, saying, Thus saith the LORD concerning Shemaiah the Nehelamite; Because that Shemaiah hath prophesied unto you, and I sent him not, and he caused you to trust in a lie:
Jeremiah 29:32

Therefore thus saith the LORD; Behold, I will punish Shemaiah the Nehelamite, and his seed: he shall not have a man to dwell among this people; neither shall he behold the good that I will do for my people, saith the LORD; because he hath taught rebellion against the LORD.
Jeremiah 29:11
For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.
corruption_summary: Jeremiah 29:11 is detached from the letter it belongs to and offered as a promise of comfortable circumstances, which is precisely the message Shemaiah the Nehelamite was punished for preaching.
corruption_paragraphs: The most-quoted verse in Jeremiah sits eighteen verses above the condemnation of a man who preached what people now take it to mean. God's thoughts of peace and the expected end are addressed to exiles who had just been told to build houses in Babylon, plant gardens, marry, and seek the peace of the city, because seventy years would pass before the return. Most of the first hearers died there. The promise was real and its horizon was a generation away, and the men who shortened it were called liars by God. To print the verse over a graduation card is to preach Shemaiah's sermon with Jeremiah's text.

The chapter also settles how false prophecy is to be identified. God's complaint against Shemaiah is not that his predictions were pessimistic or optimistic but that I sent him not, and that he caused the people to trust in a lie. Deuteronomy gave the same test: the word that does not come to pass, the LORD has not spoken. That is the ground of the dictionary's cessationism and of its warning against the modern apostle-and-prophet movements. A man who claims a word from God and is wrong has not made a forecasting error. He has, in the language of this chapter, taught rebellion against the LORD.

“Thoughts of peace, and not of evil” — in the same letter, on a seventy-year horizon.

pos: n. (the designation of two of David's mighty men)
etymology: Of uncertain origin; the Hebrew may relate to a word meaning a certain one, as though the town were left unspecified. It marks two men in the roll of David's warriors.
biblical_def: The term appears only in the registers of David's men. Helez is listed among the thirty: “Shammoth the Harorite, Helez the Pelonite” (1 Chronicles 11:27). A second bearer of the title follows further down the same roll: “Hepher the Mecherathite, Ahijah the Pelonite” (1 Chronicles 11:36). And Helez is given a month in the standing establishment of the kingdom: “The seventh captain for the seventh month was Helez the Pelonite, of the children of Ephraim: and in his course were twenty and four thousand” (1 Chronicles 27:10). Nothing else is recorded of either man — no exploit, no speech, no failure. They are named, placed, and counted. The roll they belong to is introduced with a statement of what such lists are for: “These also are the chief of the mighty men whom David had, who strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom, and with all Israel, to make him king, according to the word of the LORD concerning Israel” (1 Chronicles 11:10). Men who strengthened themselves with him — that is the whole testimony of the Pelonite, and Scripture thought it worth preserving.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Pelonite; it is a gentilic of uncertain derivation, marking a man's town or clan among David's warriors.
webster_full: PELONITE, n. The designation of Helez and of Ahijah, two of David's mighty men; the place is not certainly known.
MIGHTY, a. Having great bodily strength or physical power; very strong; valiant; bold.
ROLL, n. A register; a catalogue or official list of names.
COURSE, n. A series of appointed turns of duty; the order of succession in which men serve.
OBSCURE, a. Not noted; unknown to fame; humble; mean; living in darkness as to reputation.
scriptures: 1 Chronicles 11:27
Shammoth the Harorite, Helez the Pelonite,
1 Chronicles 11:36
Hepher the Mecherathite, Ahijah the Pelonite,
1 Chronicles 27:10
The seventh captain for the seventh month was Helez the Pelonite, of the children of Ephraim: and in his course were twenty and four thousand.
1 Chronicles 11:10

These also are the chief of the mighty men whom David had, who strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom, and with all Israel, to make him king, according to the word of the LORD concerning Israel.
corruption_summary: Obscure service is treated as service that did not matter, and a register God preserved is skimmed as though the absence of a story meant the absence of significance.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture records faithful obscurity on purpose. The Pelonite has no narrative. He killed no giant, spoke no line, and made no mistake the Chronicler thought worth reporting. What he did was strengthen himself with David in his kingdom, take the seventh month, and stand at the head of twenty-four thousand men. That is the whole account, and it is in the word of God, which is more than can be said for most of what the age considers achievement.

The application is directly against the celebrity instinct in modern church life, where significance is measured by platform and the unnamed labourer is assumed to be a lesser sort of Christian. The roll in 1 Chronicles 11 is arranged the other way. It begins with the three who broke through to fetch water from Bethlehem, and it goes on, name after name, town after town, through men about whom nothing else is known — and the introduction covers all of them alike: they made him king according to the word of the LORD. Paul's greeting lists in Romans 16 do the same thing for the church at Rome. God keeps the register.

Hebrew gibborim (H1368) — mighty men; the roll of 1 Chronicles 11.

Hebrew machaloqah (H4256) — a division or course; the seventh month.
Hebrew rosh (H7218) — head, chief; the chief of the mighty men.

“Ahijah the Pelonite” — a second man under the same designation.
“Who strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom” — what the register testifies.

etymology: The feminine gentilic of Jezreel, a town in Issachar. It belongs to Ahinoam, David's wife, and it is used to distinguish her in every list where she appears beside Abigail the Carmelitess.
biblical_def: The word attaches to one woman and always in the same pairing: “And David dwelt with Achish at Gath, he and his men, every man with his household, even David with his two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail the Carmelitess, Nabal's wife” (1 Samuel 27:3). When the Amalekites burned Ziklag, she is named among the taken: “And David's two wives were taken captives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite” (1 Samuel 30:5). And when David goes up to be made king over Judah, she goes with him: “So David went up thither, and his two wives also, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail Nabal's wife the Carmelite” (2 Samuel 2:2). She is the mother of David's firstborn: “And unto David were sons born in Hebron: and his firstborn was Amnon, of Ahinoam the Jezreelitess” (2 Samuel 3:2). The gentilic exists to keep her distinct, and the households it quietly documents are the beginning of the sorrow that fills the second half of David's reign. Amnon, born to this woman, violates his half-sister, and Absalom kills him for it, and the sword never departs from the house.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Jezreel as a city in the tribe of Issachar, a royal residence of the kings of Israel, and the valley bearing its name.
webster_full: JEZREEL, n. A city in the tribe of Issachar, a royal city of the kings of Israel, in the great plain of Esdraelon.
JEZREELITESS, n. A woman of Jezreel.
FIRSTBORN, n. The eldest child; the first in order of birth; heir by right of primogeniture.
POLYGAMY, n. A plurality of wives or husbands at the same time.
CONCUBINE, n. A woman who cohabits with a man, without the authority of a legal marriage.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 27:3
And David dwelt with Achish at Gath, he and his men, every man with his household, even David with his two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail the Carmelitess, Nabal's wife.
1 Samuel 30:5
And David's two wives were taken captives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite.
2 Samuel 2:2
So David went up thither, and his two wives also, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail Nabal's wife the Carmelite.
2 Samuel 3:2
And unto David were sons born in Hebron: and his firstborn was Amnon, of Ahinoam the Jezreelitess;
corruption_summary: David's multiple marriages are read as divine approval of polygamy, when Scripture records them without commendation and traces the ruin of his house directly through them.
corruption_paragraphs: That the Bible reports polygamy among the patriarchs and kings is sometimes offered as evidence that its sexual ethic is negotiable. The inference misreads how Scripture narrates. The creation ordinance is stated before the fall and repeated by Christ Himself: a man shall leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife, and they twain shall be one flesh. Every departure from that pattern in the Old Testament is recorded with its consequences attached — Abraham and Hagar, Jacob and the rivalry of the sisters, Elkanah's two wives and Hannah's grief, Solomon's wives turning away his heart. The law of the king had warned expressly that he should not multiply wives.

David's household is the fullest case. The lists that carefully distinguish Ahinoam the Jezreelitess from Abigail the Carmelitess are also the lists of the sons born in Hebron, and those sons destroy one another. Amnon violates Tamar; Absalom kills Amnon and then takes the kingdom; Adonijah reaches for it next. Nathan's sentence after Bathsheba — the sword shall never depart from thine house — is carried out in exactly this family. The narrative does not moralise, because it does not need to.

pos: n. (a descendant of Agag; the designation of Haman)
etymology: From Agag, the Amalekite king Saul spared and Samuel hewed in pieces. The title given to Haman places him in the line of Israel's oldest enemy, and it is repeated whenever his enmity is in view.
biblical_def: Haman is introduced with the title and it never leaves him: “After these things did king Ahasuerus promote Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him, and set his seat above all the princes that were with him” (Esther 3:1). When the signet ring passes to him the narrator adds the plainest possible gloss: “And the king took his ring from his hand, and gave it unto Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the Jews' enemy” (Esther 3:10). Esther's plea names him the same way: “And Esther spake yet again before the king, and fell down at his feet, and besought him with tears to put away the mischief of Haman the Agagite, and his device that he had devised against the Jews” (Esther 8:3). The quarrel is older than either of them. Mordecai is a Benjamite of the house of Kish, Saul's family, and Haman descends from the king Saul failed to destroy; the commission Saul disobeyed stands in 1 Samuel: “Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass” (1 Samuel 15:3). What Saul left alive came back, generations later, with a decree to exterminate his people.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Agag as a name or title of the kings of the Amalekites, and an Agagite as one descended from Agag.
webster_full: AGAG, n. A name or title borne by the kings of the Amalekites, as Pharaoh by the kings of Egypt.
AGAGITE, n. A descendant of Agag; the designation of Haman, the enemy of the Jews.
AMALEKITES, n. A people descended from Amalek, the grandson of Esau, inveterate enemies of Israel.
DEVICE, n. That which is formed by design; a scheme; a project; a stratagem, usually in a bad sense.
PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.
scriptures: Esther 3:1
After these things did king Ahasuerus promote Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him, and set his seat above all the princes that were with him.
Esther 3:10
And the king took his ring from his hand, and gave it unto Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the Jews' enemy.
Esther 8:3
And Esther spake yet again before the king, and fell down at his feet, and besought him with tears to put away the mischief of Haman the Agagite, and his device that he had devised against the Jews.
1 Samuel 15:3
Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.
corruption_summary: Esther is read as a secular court romance because God is not named in it, and the deliberate genealogical frame that makes it a chapter in a much older war is passed over.
corruption_paragraphs: The absence of the divine name from Esther has led to the book being treated as the least theological in the canon — a nationalist tale, a court intrigue, a festival legend. The genealogies refuse that reading. Mordecai is identified as a Benjamite, son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish; Haman is identified four times as the Agagite. Those are not decorations. They put a descendant of Saul's house opposite a descendant of the king Saul spared, and they make the book the settlement of a commission left undone in 1 Samuel 15. God is unnamed and He is not absent; the whole plot turns on a sleepless night and a book of records read aloud.

The hard text behind it is the herem commanded against Amalek, which modern readers find intolerable and often use to indict the Old Testament. Scripture gives the reason: Amalek attacked the feeble and the weary at the rear of Israel coming out of Egypt, and God swore war with Amalek from generation to generation. The command was judicial, given to one nation, at one time, for a stated cause, and it is never a warrant for anything since. Saul's partial obedience — sparing the king and the best of the sheep while calling it obedience — is the text where Samuel says that to obey is better than sacrifice, and Esther is the long invoice for it.

pos: n. (the designation of Elijah the prophet)
etymology: From Tishbe, a settlement whose location is uncertain; the text places the man among the inhabitants of Gilead, east of Jordan. The title belongs to Elijah alone and appears at every hinge of his ministry.
biblical_def: Elijah enters Scripture without genealogy, introduction, or call narrative — only a hometown and a sentence: “And Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the inhabitants of Gilead, said unto Ahab, As the LORD God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word” (1 Kings 17:1). The title returns at the two moments when the word of the LORD sends him against a king. After Naboth's vineyard: “And the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying” (1 Kings 21:17). And after Ahab humbles himself: “And the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying” (1 Kings 21:28). The phrase he uses of himself in his first sentence is the key to the man: before whom I stand. He is a servant standing in a court, and the court is not Ahab's. The New Testament takes pains to say he was nothing more than a man: “Elias was a man subject to like passions as we are, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain: and it rained not on the earth by the space of three years and six months” (James 5:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Tishbe as a place in Gilead, whence Elijah is called the Tishbite.
webster_full: TISHBITE, n. An inhabitant of Tishbe, a place in Gilead; the designation of Elijah the prophet.
PROPHET, n. One that foretells future events; one who speaks by divine inspiration, or by the direction of God.
DROUGHT, n. Dryness; want of rain or of water; thirst; want of drink.
ZEAL, n. Passionate ardor in the pursuit of any thing; in general, ardor in the pursuit of good.
PASSIONS, n. Susceptibility of impressions from external agents; the feelings of a man liable to be moved.
scriptures: 1 Kings 17:1

And Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the inhabitants of Gilead, said unto Ahab, As the LORD God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.
1 Kings 21:17
And the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying,
1 Kings 21:28
And the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying,
James 5:17
Elias was a man subject to like passions as we are, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain: and it rained not on the earth by the space of three years and six months.
corruption_summary: Elijah is either inflated into a superhuman figure whose experience is beyond ordinary believers, or reduced to a folk hero whose miracles are literary decoration.
corruption_paragraphs: James anticipated the first error and closed it deliberately: Elias was a man subject to like passions as we are. The narrative itself supplies the evidence — after the fire fell on Carmel and the prophets of Baal were slain, one message from Jezebel sent him a day's journey into the wilderness asking to die. God's treatment of him there is the pastoral heart of the story: he is allowed to sleep, fed twice by an angel, and only then questioned. The point of including the collapse is that the man who shut heaven by prayer was not made of different material from the reader.

The second error handles the drought and the fire as symbol rather than event. Scripture does not permit it. James dates the drought — three years and six months — and our Lord cites the widow of Sarepta as a historical instance of sovereign election, telling the synagogue at Nazareth that many widows were in Israel in the days of Elias and unto none of them was he sent save unto one, a Gentile. That is how the New Testament reads the Tishbite: as a real man in a real famine, sent where God chose to send him, and standing all his life before the God whose court he had named in his first recorded sentence.
